awd_titl_txt: CAS: Electrochemical Processes of Chelated Metals
awd_abstract_narration:
In this project, funded by the Chemical Structure, Dynamics & Mechanisms B Program of the Chemistry Division, Professor Michael Marshak of the Department of Chemistry at the University of Colorado Boulder is developing new materials for grid-scale long duration energy storage. Grid-scale energy storage is a longstanding and unmet need to support the sustainable production of electricity from intermittent sources such as wind and solar. Flow batteries offer a compelling engineering framework for providing inexpensive energy storage because they permit independent scaling of their power conversion and energy storage components. This project supports investigation of the fundamental electrochemical behavior of metal chelate materials as sustainable and scalable energy storage materials in flow batteries. This project also supports the development of new education and outreach programs in battery chemistry, with the goal of creating a competitive and equitable US workforce in clean energy technologies.

The goal of the project aims to provide a fundamental molecular understanding of a broad class of metal chelate coordination complexes, coupled with the evaluation of these chemical phenomena to improve system level flow battery performance. This understanding will be accomplished through the evaluation of the ability of organic chelates to inhibit water splitting reactions and test its performance limits. This approach will then be expanded to develop metal chelate complexes that can undergo multi-electron redox reactions, which can further increase the energy density and performance of the flow battery systems. This project represents a new approach to address longstanding challenges in the field of energy storage with low-cost materials that are economically feasible for wide scale deployment. Moreover, this project not only could prove transformative for enabling high-voltage aqueous batteries, but the molecular inhibition of water splitting using chelates could also carry wider implications for controlling hydrogen evolution reactions in other electrochemical and electrocatalytic applications such as electrochemical fuel production.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
Flow batteries store electricity in liquids held in tanks. To charge the battery, the liquids are pumped through a device called a flow cell, where they absorb electrical energy. To discharge it, they flow back through the flow cell and release that energy. Because the energy is stored in the tanks, storing more just takes bigger tanks. That makes flow batteries a good fit for supplying power for many hours at a time, at the scale of the power grid. The liquids are mostly water, so they cannot catch fire, and the systems are built to last for decades.

For the electric grid, this kind of storage means more reliable and affordable power. A flow battery can charge when demand is low and deliver power during peak hours, equipment failures or extreme weather. It can be installed close to homes, hospitals, factories and data centers. It can also help utilities meet rising electricity demand without waiting years for new power lines.

This project studied how organic molecules called chelates change the behavior of metals. A chelate wraps around a metal atom, changing the metal's voltage, its stability, and how it reacts with water. Our team made and studied chelated forms of chromium, cerium, and vanadium. We isolated a strongly energized chromium compound that stays stable in water, which is key to building higher-voltage batteries. We showed that chelation can get more out of vanadium, a costly metal. We also found that small differences in a chelate's shape can improve battery efficiency. Finally, we showed how designing flow batteries for safety and location, not just compactness, opens up new places to install them. Together, these results give researchers design rules for building batteries from abundant, low-cost metals.

The project trained three graduate students in battery research, including chemical synthesis, electrochemistry, and building and testing batteries. These skills are in high demand as U.S. battery manufacturing grows. The team also developed a low-cost lab method for measuring metals, published for use in college chemistry courses.

This work supports national priorities in American energy leadership, a reliable and secure power grid, domestic manufacturing and a skilled technical workforce.
